successors.name: Tibetans (Era of Fragmentation)
successors.text: the Tibetan plateau and the Hexi Corridor, held by the rival Tibetan lords after Langdarma's death, without the Dzungaria and Turfan land the Uyghurs had taken in 790-792

ledger.x: 618: Songtsen Gampo succeeds the assassinated Namri Songtsen and the Tibetan Empire begins.
628: the plateau widens north and east.
638: the north-eastern edge moves toward Songzhou.
666: Khotan and the southern Tarim rim.
670: the fight for the Four Garrisons begins.
679: Pei Xingjian wins the Tarim back.
687: the Tibetans take the Western Regions again.
692: the first Tarim war ends with the Anxi Protectorate re-established at Qiuci.
704: the Mywa peoples of Yunnan submit.
717: the fight for Aksu and the Stone City.
722: Tang restores the king of Gilgit.
749: the fight for the Stone City ends in a Tang recovery.
763: the second fight for the Tarim begins: Yanqi 763, Qiuci 787, the garrisons 790, Yutian 792, with Anxi and Beiting cut off from the Tang after 764.
763: the Tibetans leave Chang'an after 'fifteen days'.
764: the fight for Hexi and Longyou begins and runs to the 783 treaty.
787: Qiuci falls to Tibet for the last time.
790: the Uyghurs fight the Tibetans for Beiting and Turfan, a war that runs to 823.
792: the second Tarim contest ends with the whole Tarim in Tibetan hands.
792: the Uyghurs take Gaochang and Beiting.
842: Langdarma is assassinated and the empire breaks apart.

wars.name: Tibetan attack on Songzhou
wars.outcome: Songtsen Gampo's embassy of 634 asked for a marriage alliance; when it was refused Tibet attacked Tang affiliates in 637 and 638 and the frontier city of Songzhou.

wars.name: Tibetan conquest of Zhangzhung
wars.outcome: Zhangzhung submitted in 634 (Tang Annals) or was overrun in 645 (Stein); it disappeared as a kingdom.

wars.name: Tibetan conquest of the Tuyuhun
wars.outcome: 'In 635-36, the Emperor attacked and defeated the Tuyuhun ('Azha)'; the kingdom 'was defeated by the Tibetan army and gradually assimilated into Tibetan culture' in 663 (669 on the Tang-Tibet relations page).

wars.name: Tang-Tibetan war for the Four Garrisons
wars.outcome: Tibet won at Dafei River in 670 and held the Tarim; the Tang retook Qiuci in 673, lost it in 677, won in 679 under Pei Xingjian, withdrew in 686, lost the region in 687 and recovered it under Wang Xiaojie in 692.

wars.name: Tibetan campaigns in Gilgit and Baltistan
wars.outcome: Attacks on Lesser Bolü in 656 and on Wakhan; Tibetan conquests of Gilgit in 710 and 737, a Tang restoration in 722 and Gao Xianzhi's capture in 747; in 754 'Tang forces defeated Baltistan (Greater Bolü) and Tibetan forces'.

wars.name: Tibetan-Tang fighting over Aksu and the Stone City
wars.outcome: Tibetan attacks on the Stone City in 694, 717, 720 (seized), 741 (sacked); Tang defeat there in 745; Tang recovery in 749.

wars.name: Tianbao War
wars.outcome: Nanzhao captured 32 native counties in 750, turned to Tibet when the Tang refused peace, and with the Tibetans destroyed Li Mi's 70,000 in 754; the Tang could not attack Nanzhao again.

wars.name: Tibetan capture of Chang'an
wars.outcome: The Tibetans reached Chang'an in late 763 and occupied it for fifteen days.

wars.name: Tibetan conquest of Hexi and Anxi
wars.outcome: Liang Prefecture fell in 764, cutting off Anxi and Beiting; Shazhou in 786; the last Anxi garrisons by 790 and Yutian in 792.

wars.name: Uyghur-Tibetan war
wars.outcome: The Tibetans beat the Uyghurs and Tang at Tingzhou in 790 but the Uyghurs won at Beiting in 791 and took Gaochang in 792; they seized Liang Province in 808, a Tibetan raid reached within two days of Ordu-Baliq in 816, a Tibetan force was repulsed in 821 and…

wars.name: Battle of Shenchuan
wars.outcome: Nanzhao broke with Tibet and switched to the Tang; in 795 Yimouxun attacked a Tibetan stronghold in 'Kunming' and in 801 the Tibetan force was beaten at Dulu.

wars.name: Tibetan civil war after Langdarma
wars.outcome: After Langdarma's death 'the two princes Yumtan and Osung ... fought for the throne and initiated a civil war'; the Battle of U-Yor led to the collapse of the empire.

certainty.note: The plateau, the Tarim, Gilgit and the Yunnan marches were approximate lines; the Tang frontier by Long Mountain and the Chiling boundary monument (731, Tang-Tibet relations page) were agreed lines but their courses are not on the pages.
The Tang-Tibetan frontier is sharp from the 783 treaty that 'defined the borders' and the 821/822 treaty, but no page gives its course; the Uyghur, Tarim and Yunnan frontiers stay soft.
